summary: The note argues that local inventors are pivotal to building smart cities because they understand their cities' specific challenges. It profiles inventors across US cities working on water, energy, mobility, waste and public health, and covers how public partnerships, education programs and supportive policy can nurture them. It concludes that grassroots innovation, backed by governments, businesses and communities, drives sustainable and inclusive urban technology.
one_line: Local inventors across US cities are building smart-city technologies, and partnerships, education and supportive policy can amplify their impact.
key_facts: John K. Baxter of Austin, Texas developed a rainwater harvesting system that integrates with city buildings, conserves water and eases pressure on the city's drainage system during heavy rainfall.
Angela Martinez of Boston, Massachusetts devised a modular pavement technology, now being piloted, to reduce Boston's urban heat island effect.
Rachel Nguyen of San Francisco, California invented a compact, solar-powered device that captures fog and turns it into drinkable water; it has been in testing since October 2023.
Elijah Green's energy-harvesting sidewalks in Atlanta, Georgia use pedestrians' kinetic energy to power streetlights and Wi-Fi stations, and have operated since late 2023.
Sarah Chen's public transportation app in Portland, Oregon launched in November 2023 and uses real-time data to streamline bus and train routes, reducing congestion and waiting times.

Aaron Gomez of Phoenix, Arizona engineered a cost-effective, solar-powered cooling system for public spaces, with a projected decrease in heat-related health incidents and an increase in foot traffic.
Daniel Kim's waste-to-energy conversion plant in Minneapolis began operations in January 2024, turning local organic waste into biogas, reducing landfill usage and creating jobs.
Lila Thompson partnered with New York City's Department of Environmental Protection on a smart sensor network monitoring water quality and consumption across Manhattan, implemented in February 2024.
In Detroit, Michigan, former automotive engineer Michael Clark worked with the city to develop a fleet of autonomous electric vehicles serving underserved neighborhoods.
Catherine Zhao's "Tech for Tomorrow" youth initiative in Denver, Colorado, begun in late 2023, trains young people in STEM problem-solving for urban technologies.
Ethan Brown started the "Urban Innovate Hub" in Seattle, Washington in September 2023 as a collaboration space for inventors, hobbyists and professionals.
Nashville introduced a local innovation fund in October 2023 to give grants to inventors working on urban technology projects.
San Diego's "Tech Growth Initiative" offers mentoring and business development services to help local inventors turn prototypes into marketable products.
